To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
climate change-induced wetland CH4 emission feedbacks to climate change will dominate anthropogenic 21 st century CH4 emissions by the end of this century.

climate-change-induced increases in borealand tropical CH4 emissions are projected to dominate anthropogenic CH 4 emissions by the end of 21st century, with a range of 38 to 58% under different scenarios.

climate change-induced expansion of wetlands, together with temperature-driven increases in CH4 emissions from tropical and boreal wetlands, will exceed anthropogenic CH4 emission by 38 to >56% in the 21st Century, depending on the climate change scenario.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of global methane emissions from wetlands in climate change.
the role of global warming and wetland methane emissions on climate change in the 21st Century.
the role of global methane (CH4), which is the second most important greenhouse gas after CO2.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

wetland CH4 emission feedbacks to climate change are an important component in the climate system and should be represented as a key factor in climate change mitigation policies aiming to keep warming below 2° C.
the climate change induced expansion of wetland CH 4 emissions will be an important driver of climate change and must be represented in policies to reduce climate change.
wetland methane (CH 4 ) emissions are a significant component of the global CH 4 budget.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
climate change and wetland CH 4 feedbacks are an important component in climate change.
wetland CH4 emission feedbacks are important in climate change and should not be neglected in climate mitigation policies.

the climate change-induced expansion of global wetlands and the associated CH4 emissions will be a significant contributor to future climate warming, and should be considered in mitigation policies aiming to keep global warming below 1.5 to 2 °C.
The main takeaway from our work is that

climate-change and CH4 wetland feedbacks to radiance forcing are an important contribution to climate change and should therefore be represented in policies that aim to limit global warming below 2100.
climate change will increase global CH4 emissions, with a large contribution from global wetlands.
climate mitigation policies should consider mitigation of wetlands CH4 emissions.
